newsitem.title: USA: GM sales rose 6 percent, Chrysler fell 9 percent.
newsitem.headline: GM sales rose 6 percent, Chrysler fell 9 percent.

text.p: General Motors Corp. Friday posted an unexpected 6 percent jump in U.S. sales for July, but Toyota and Honda continued to outperform its American rivals. Sales at Chrysler Corp. fell 9 percent in July.

GM, the world's largest automaker, said higher incentive spending on older models drove sales up sharply in the latest month. GM sold 419,102 cars and trucks in July, up from 393,526 a year earlier. Car sales rose 3 percent to 237,267, while total truck sales shot up 11.5 percent to 181,835.

Analysts had expected GM to post a total decline of about 4 percent. But GM sales surged in the last two weeks of the month, allowing the automaker to report higher sales in every division except Oldsmobile.
GM officials cited a recovery from work stoppages, strong sales of newer models and a change in how it spends incentive money to clear out cars and trucks.

The company eliminated the traditional 5 percent discount it gives dealers on every carryover model in late September or early October. In its place, GM began offering lower finance rates of 2.9 percent or cash rebates ranging from $750 to $1,500 on many of its older cars.
"I think we were just caught off guard a bit in terms of how aggressive our competitors were," said Michael DiGiovanni, who oversees GM's market research and vehicle forecasts.

Reversing June's poor results, GM truck sales were the best ever for a July, with both Chevrolet and GMC setting monthly records. Also up were GM's minivan sales, which company officials said was proof the new Venture, Trans Sport and Silhoutte are catching on with consumers.
Meanwhile, Toyota Motor Corp. and Honda Motor Co. Ltd. continued to outpace Detroit's Big Three.
Toyota sales rose 14.6 percent to 108,939 vehicles while July sales at Honda's American unit soared 31.8 percent to 87,929, a monthly record.
"Hot cars and a hot economy equal record sales," Dick Colliver, Honda division executive vice president, said in a statement.

While the results from Honda and Toyota impressed analysts, Christopher Cedergren at consultant Nextrend in Thousand Oaks, Calif., said the numbers also reflected higher incentives to clear out 1997 models.
"They had an aggressive marketing push," he said.

Sales of the popular Civic jumped 51 percent to 29,995, while Accord sales rose 10 percent to 33,865. The Toyota Camry further cemented its lead as the best-selling U.S. car so far this year with an 8.7 percent sales gain in July to 32,555, its best July ever.
At Chrysler, July vehicle sales fell to 199,662 from 220,139 as the company continued to face tough comparisons with strong year-ago levels.
Overall truck sales for the U.S. No. 3 automaker fell 8 percent to 134,858. Total car sales were 64,804, a decline of 13 percent.

"Some of the totals are lagging a bit behind last year's records, but the market is solid and we're seeing strength in sales of our key products," James Holden, executive vice president of sales and marketing, said in a statement.
Chrysler said minivan sales for the month were 50,547, up 1 percent from last year's 50,156 and a monthly record.
Ford Motor Co. is scheduled to report sales Aug. 5.
